title: Thermal Hall tomography of chiral superconductivity in rhombohedral graphene
abstract: A chiral superconductor carries chiral Majorana modes along its edges, and a single integer, the Bogoliubov--de Gennes Chern number, counts them. Thirty years of candidate materials have not yielded a measurement of that integer, because the magnetic signatures usually invoked are not topologically protected. Rhombohedral graphene makes the question both urgent and answerable: magnetic imaging resolves rewritable time-reversal-breaking domains inside the superconducting phase, while quantum oscillations reveal a normal state too intricate to reconstruct pocket by pocket. We show that the low-temperature thermal Hall conductance returns the integer directly, with no such reconstruction. For band-projected pairing it equals the pairing-vortex winding enclosed by the occupied regions of momentum space. Splitting the intravalley Hamiltonian into symmetric and antisymmetric parts isolates the trigonal warping and finite Cooper pair momentum of the real material: the antisymmetric part is topologically inert, direct Chern calculations across $525$ parameter points show the invariant preserved, and one inequality marks where a Bogoliubov Fermi surface removes quantization. The plateau $κ_{xy}/T=(π^2k_B^2/6h)\,C_{\rm BdG}$ then reads out the integer, its sign reverses with the imaged domain, a written domain wall should carry $2|C_{\rm BdG}|$ Majorana channels, and the thermometry required already resolves single thermal quanta in encapsulated graphene at millikelvin temperatures.
summary: The paper develops a theoretical framework showing that the thermal Hall conductance of chiral superconductors is quantized and directly measures the system's topological invariant, the Chern number. Using graphene as a model, they predict that $\kappa_{xy}/T$ reads out this integer, offering a powerful diagnostic tool for detecting exotic superconducting phases.
main_problem: The primary goal is to measure the Bogoliubov–de Gennes Chern number ($	ext{CBdG}$), an integer characterizing chiral Majorana modes in superconductors, which has proven difficult using traditional magnetic signatures.
main_result: The low-temperature thermal Hall conductance ($\kappa_{xy}/T$) directly reads out this topological integer $	ext{CBdG}$, providing a robust diagnostic tool for chiral superconductivity. The sign of this plateau reverses when imaging domain walls, confirming the topological nature of the state.
method: Theoretical calculations employing the Kubo formula approach on the BdG Hamiltonian are used to predict quantized thermal transport coefficients based on calculated Chern numbers derived from momentum-space winding rules.
model_or_system: The study focuses on chiral superconductivity, modeled using rhombohedral graphene. The theory utilizes the Bogoliubov-de Gennes (BdG) framework, splitting the Hamiltonian into symmetric and antisymmetric parts to isolate physical effects like trigonal warping and finite Cooper pair momentum.
key_observables: Low-temperature thermal Hall conductance ($\kappa_{xy}/T$), Chern number ($	ext{CBdG}$), Bogoliubov Fermi surface gap ($\delta_{BdG}$).
important_parameters: Temperature ($T$), pairing amplitude ($\Delta$), graphene warping strength, and the vortex winding enclosed by occupied regions in momentum space.
main_assumptions: The quantization of $\kappa_{xy}/T$ is assumed to hold at low temperatures, and the analysis relies on mapping topological invariants (Chern number) onto measurable transport quantities.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the finite-temperature response framework showing quantized plateaus for different Chern numbers ($	ext{CBdG}=1, 2$), and show how the thermal Hall conductance is related to the topological invariant.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the theoretical link between the chiral topology (Chern number) and the measurable low-temperature thermal Hall conductance. It details the Hamiltonian decomposition for graphene, calculates the Chern number using momentum-space winding rules, and predicts the quantized plateau $\kappa_{xy}/T \propto 	ext{CBdG}$.
why_interesting: This work provides a highly specific, experimentally testable prediction ($\kappa_{xy}/T$ quantization) linking abstract topological invariants (Chern numbers) to measurable transport properties in condensed matter systems.
